title: Optical Fourier Architecture for Universal Nonlinear Functions
authors: Martin F. X. Mauser, Joshua Morris, Sara Galatro, Philip Walther, Borivoje Dakic
abstract: We introduce an exact algebraic architecture that evaluates an arbitrary finite Fourier series using a two-mode ($2 \times 2$) linear optical circuit, with the only tunable components being single-mode phase shifters encoding the function argument. We prove that such a circuit must exist for every Fourier series and derive an analytical method for its construction based on spectral factorisation. The resulting optical system exhibits an $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth for an $N$-harmonic expansion, executing function evaluations in the passive optical time-of-flight. Finally, we validate our claims numerically, demonstrating that even for sequences with thousands of Fourier terms, our proposed circuit construction correctly synthesises continuous and discontinuous nonlinear functions. Our architecture thus provides a universal, deterministic foundation for single-variable nonlinear optical computing on integrated photonic platforms.
summary: This work presents a deterministic, lossless method to build an optical circuit that computes any function represented by a finite Fourier series. By leveraging spectral factorization and Cholesky decomposition, the authors construct the necessary optical unitaries layer-by-layer. This establishes a universal, scalable foundation for nonlinear optical computation using integrated photonics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of evaluating an arbitrary finite Fourier series using only linear optical components, aiming to achieve universal, deterministic nonlinear optical computing.
main_result: It proves that such a lossless optical circuit always exists and provides an $O(N)$ depth construction method for an $N$-harmonic expansion.
method: The construction relies on an exact algebraic method derived from spectral factorization, which requires finding a complementary polynomial $g(z)$ such that $|f(z)|^2 + |g(z)|^2 = C$.
model_or_system: The physical system is a two-mode ($2 	imes 2$) linear optical circuit implemented on integrated photonic circuits. The computation is modeled by the evolution of a fixed input state $|\phiangle$ through a sequence of tunable phase shifters and fixed unitaries.
key_observables: The optical amplitude in a fixed output mode, proportional to the target function $\hat{f}(z)$.
important_parameters: The circuit depth scales as $O(N)$ for an $N$-harmonic expansion; the input power $C$ must be greater than the maximum value of $|\hat{f}(z)|^2$ on the unit circle.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the target function can be represented by a finite Fourier series and operates entirely on classical coherent optical amplitudes, avoiding nonlinear materials.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the general optical circuit ansatz. Figure 3 benchmarks three spectral factorization algorithms (Algebraic root-pairing, Cholesky, Szegő-Kolmogorov) comparing runtime scaling and spectral unitary residuals for smooth and staircase functions.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the necessary algebraic condition ($|f|^2 + |g|^2 = C$) using the Fejér-Riesz theorem. It then details the deterministic computation of $g(z)$ via Cholesky factorization of a Toeplitz matrix, followed by an iterative, layer-by-layer construction of the required unitary optical circuit.
why_interesting: While the core physics is in optics, the rigorous mathematical machinery—spectral factorization, Toeplitz matrix decomposition, and deterministic circuit synthesis—is highly relevant to quantum information theory and quantum computation, particularly in photonic quantum computing architectures.

FIG. 2: Optical encoding of a function. (a) Conceptual compilation pipeline: an arbitrary target function is approximated by a truncated Fourier series, with the quality of the approximation depending on the number of terms and the target function. Given any such series, we generate by algebraic spectral factorisation a sequence of MZIs and single-mode phase shifters that, when acting on a fixed optical input, produce the desired approximating function output ˆf(x).
